analytic.title: Methodology of Combining Empirical Stress Testing and Formal-Methods Based Schedulability Analysis for Real-Time Multicore Software

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Current certification guidance documents for aircraft provide plans, processes, and objectives. This has been successful in terms of achieving safety but it comes at the expense of leading to a less agile software development; this makes software development slow for greenfield development, prevents rapid updates of software, and prevents rapid upgrades of hardware. The use of formal methods (FM) has the potential to avoid some of these drawbacks. A critical issue today is the use of multicore and their potential to introduce inter-core interference which can violate real-time requirements. Therefore, in this paper, we present a two-step reasoning framework that can be used to bring some FM to the analysis of real-time requirements of software executing on multicore.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Current certification guidance documents for aircraft provide plans, processes, and objectives (see [1,44] or Chapter 15 in [43]). Plans include activities and these are subject to process audit [2]. The certification objectives are supported by "tried-and-true" design principles that achieves or improves determinism. There is often disagreement on the meaning of the word determinism but it often means one of the following:
• The timing and computed result do not depend on randomness (or is less dependent on randomness).
• The timing and computed result of one component does not depend on other components (or is less dependent on other components).
• If the system or component is described as a state-machine, then its state is fully visible and controllable (or as controllable as possible).
• If replication is used for fault-tolerance, then all replicas are initialized to the same state, fed the same input, and fed inputs at the same time (or with as small difference as possible).
• It is possible to predict or prove properties of interest.

A component is typically assigned a criticality level that determines the level of rigor in design, implementation, and testing. Testing and reviews are often used to gain confidence in the validity of bi-directional traceability between requirements on different levels (system requirement↔high-level requirement, high-level requirement ↔low-level requirement, low-level requirement ↔source code). There is also traceability between tests, rest results, and requirements. In terms of safety, this has been very successful: the number of accidents today is much smaller than it was decades ago (see [3] or page 1 in 11]).

Despite the successful track record of the current certification paradigm, it brings with it the following drawbacks. First, it restricts the freedom of software practitioners from using designs and working principles as they see fit. Second, it makes software development slow for greenfield development, prevents rapid updates of software, and prevents rapid upgrades of hardware. This is because for a software system, the number of possible executions tends to grow exponentially with the input space and also grow exponentially with the number of states as well. This exponential growth is unfortunate because the size of the software itself grows exponentially toosee Section 3 in [32]. Testing is sometimes used to establish validity of the traceability; in this case testing is not applied to the entire software system and this can have the benefit of having smaller input space and smaller state-space to cover; but the exponential dependence remains. Thus, the number of test cases required for exhaustive testing is so large that exhaustive testing is not practicable. In practice, one uses extensive nonexhaustive methods (such as code coverage criterion) for those reasons, as practitioners have long come to find out, and others suggest to employ formal model of software system. The use of extensive non-exhaustive testing is problematic for two reasons. First, it is expensive. Software testing accounts for approximately 50% of the cost of software system development [33]. Second, it leads to long development cycles. Long development cycle is problematic in the commercial sector because it prolongs time-to-market. But it is also problematic in DoD because one of the main priorities in DoD is rapid fielding while maintaining a high level of software assurance [25,26,27,28,29].

There are several techniques to reduce the number of test cases. These techniques were developed for testing whether the computer program computes the right result. Unfortunately, they tend to be less effective for testing whether timing requirements are satisfied (even in software systems with a single thread). We discuss this now. A common technique to reduce the number of test cases is to partition the input space so that all executions in the same partition have the same or similar behavior. For example, consider two different inputs to a program so that they execute the same path in a control-flow graph of the program. It is tempting to put them in the same partition of the input space and argue that only one of these inputs is needed in a test suite. However, the executions corresponding to these two inputs may operate on different data and hence may produce different outputs. Moreover, from the perspective of real-time requirements, the executions corresponding to these two inputs may access memory locations differently and hence may exercise the cache memory differently. Hence, these two inputs may have different timing behavior. Furthermore, even if two inputs to the same process cause the process to execute the same path in the control flow graph and these two inputs causes the execution time of this process to be identical, then it can still happen that these inputs cause the process to influence other processes in different ways (e.g., one input causes another process to experience a large amount of cache eviction but another input does not). The research community has created several techniques for testing (e.g., creating a test suite that satisfies MC/DC criterion [4] is a common one) but as can be seen they do not offer 100% safety. Hence, investigating alternative evaluation techniques or approaches is worthwhile.

An alternative approach is to (as much as possible) use formal methods (FMs); that is, try to create a formal model of the software system, specify correctness properties, and use formal methods to prove, mathematically, that the correctness properties hold for the formal model. Correct FM and its correct use yield 100% safety but there are several reasons why this may not always be the case; these include:
• The formal model may be different from reality and hence a proof of correctness may not apply to reality.
• Humans may make mistakes in specifying correctness properties.
• The FM may rely on a tool that has defects (e.g., states that a correctness property is true although it is false).

• The execution of a FM tool may rely on other components that are faulty (e.g., a file that the FM tool takes as input may be corrupted; a FM tool may use a parsing library to read a file format and this parsing library may be defective).

• The output of a FM tool may be misunderstood by a human (e.g., if a FM tool outputs true, does it mean that the correctness property is true; or does it mean that it is true that there is an execution that violates the correctness property?).

• The time for a FM tool to finish execution may be so long that it is longer than the time that a software practitioner is willing to wait. Also, the resources (e.g., main memory) required by a FM tool may be greater than what is available.
In addition, there are several obstacles for practitioners to use FM; these include:
• FM requires that humans learn how to use them and it may be that the upfront investment in learning is perceived to be not worth it.
• There are different types of correctness properties and different FM tools and it may be hard for software practitioner to know which one(s) to use (if any).

Nonetheless, FM appear to be the best way forward for simultaneously achieving safety and rapid software development. Some voices in the research literature agrees. For example, Page 7 in [9] points out that "Simulation and testing simply cannot accomplish this [total exploration of the entire state space] in practical amounts of time" and [10] argues that we cannot get safe enough aircraft with digital computers if we just rely on testing. Similarly, page 5 in [42] states: "We can never test all threads through the system with all possible inputs [5]" It is noteworthy that the weakness of testing is inherent (exponential number of test cases) whereas the weakness of FM is accidental (depends on maturity of FM tools and underlying theories); hence the weakness of the latter can be expected to decrease over time. Put it differently: over time, FM becomes more viable. Therefore, in this paper, we discuss FMs for aircraft certification. We do not discuss FM in general; we focus on real-time properties of software executing on multicore processors. To this end, we present a methodology that uses a FM to prove correct timing given a model of a set of processes. The characteristics of these processes are specified by numeric parameters, and these are obtained through empirical testing. The general ideas of this methodology are hardly new; similar ideas are routinely used in the academic research literature on real-time systems. But we present it here because (i) we have found that there is a large gap between academic theory and practice of software developers/certifiers, and (ii) we believe there is value in reducing this gap.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II gives background. Section III shows the two-step reasoning framework. Section IV shows it for single-core. Section V shows it for multicore. Section VI concludes.

div.head: A. Formal methods
div.p: Fig. 1 shows a generic FM. A FM takes as input a model and a correctness property. We let M denote the model and ϕ denote the correctness property. The intent is that M represents either (i) an as-built software system or (ii) an as-planned-tobe-built software system. Early in the design process, M may represent an as-planned-to-be-built software system. When the software system has been fully developed, however, M may represent the as-built software system. A FM can be applied in a software development process that uses Model-Base Software Engineering (MBSE) using AADL [5]. In this case, an AADL model describes the design (components, threads, finite state machines, source code) and generates an instance model within AADL. From this instance model, one can extract the information needed for a specific FM tool for a specific correctness property; this extracted information can be thought of as M. A model M does not need to be extracted from an instance model and it is possible to use FMs even without using MBSE. For example, M can be created manually (e.g., from design documents, requirements documents, source code, executable code).

Typically, a correctness property ϕ makes a claim about all executions that are possible in M. Some correctness properties are called liveness properties meaning that for all possible executions, the correctness property expresses that eventually something will be true (e.g., if a process performs wait on a semaphore, then eventually the process will enter the critical section). Other correctness properties are called safety properties, meaning that for all possible executions, the correctness property expresses that at all times, something is true. Note that the latter makes a statement about at-all-times whereas the former makes a statement about eventually. In this paper, we focus on safety properties.

A FM tool outputs an answer "yes" or "no" or "undecided." If it outputs "yes" then it means that the FM guarantees that property ϕ holds for all executions that are possible in M. Analogously, if it outputs "no" then it means that the FM has found that the property ϕ does not holds for all executions that are possible in M. Another way to express it is that: if it outputs "no," then it means that the FM tool has found that there exists an execution that is possible in M such that for this execution the property ϕ does not hold. There is currently an increasing interest in explainable FM; that is, the FM tool does not just output Yes/No/Undecided based on a question, but it also outputs an explanation to the answer output [20]. This area is in its infancy though so we will not discuss it in this paper.

There is a rich scientific area which provides tools assuming that M is described as a finite state machine (FSM) and ϕ is described in the language temporal logicsee [6]. They rely on two concepts: reachable states and error states. The set of reachable states is the set of states such that there is a sequence such that the first state in the sequence is an initial state, the last state in the sequence is in the reachable states, and for each adjacent pair in the sequence, it is possible for the FSM to make that transition. A set of error states are those states in which the correctness property is false. Many of these tools work as follows: (i) compute the set of reachable states (or an overapproximation of it), (ii) compute the set of error states (or an overapproximation of it), and (iii) check if these sets intersect; if they do not, then we can be certain that the correctness property is true. These tools have the advantage of being very expressive but they come with the drawback that they often have poor scalability (i.e., it can take a very long time for them to produce an output). Many of these tools focus on the case that the correctness property (ϕ) is about the value domain (i.e., computing the right result). There is also an extension (called timed-automata) which allows a finite state machine to also describe clocks and the progression of time; but it suffers from poor scalability too [7,8].

To prove correctness of timing and get better scalability, we will discuss another form of FM. To do so, we start by discussing why timing matters, what causes delays in software systems and then present a two-step reasoning framework.

div.head: B. Why timing matters?
div.p: Timing is emphasized in safety standards (e.g., DO-178C [1]) and the literature (e.g., page 4 in [12]). It also emphasizes (page 2 in [12]) that it is important that timing requirements are satisfied for all possible conditions (robustness) and that : Timing problems are one of the common causes of runtime failures in process-control systems, and timing is often inadequately specified. (page 8 in [12]) Some visible failures may appear to be non-timing failures, but their root cause is a timing fault. Examples of this include:

• A program (called "timing bomb" [13]) where a program performs periodic sampling and when sampling also reads current time so that each sample has a timestamp. The program computes the difference between two consecutive samples and computes the difference between the timestamps of these consecutive samples; this yields an estimate of the rate of change of a physical variable (e.g., estimate of a time-derivative of a signal). Unfortunately, on some platforms, the clock has poor resolution and then it can happen that these two timestamps are identical; this results in the difference between these two timestamps being zero, when it's not. Hence, the program performs division by zero and crashes (hence, the name "time bomb"). • The NASA Ingenuity helicopter, used during the most recent mission on Mars, suffered from a lost image frame and faulty timestamps and this caused it to almost lose control [14].
These examples are due to programming errors related to timing. However, other timing issues are caused by resource contention causing delay; we now discuss this.
We are often interested in the time delay from the occurrence of one event until the occurrence of another event. Fig. 2 shows it. The following exemplify this:
• In a feedback control system, we are often interested in the delay from sensing to actuation (because if this is too large, then the feedback control system may become unstable).

• In a filter that estimates the state (e.g., location, orientation, and their associated time derivatives) of a physical object that we control (such as our own aircraft), we are often interested in making sure that a computation based on a sensor reading and most recent state finishes before a new sensor data becomes available (because otherwise one data item may be overwritten).

• In a filter that estimates the state (e.g., location, orientation, and their time derivatives) of a physical object that we do not control (e.g., another aircraft or missile), we often want to formulate a set of hypotheses of the state; the larger this set is the more uncertainty we have in our estimate. In this way, if we get new sensor data but skip their processing, then the uncertainty of the estimate becomes larger. Hence, it is beneficial for such software to execute contiguously to maintain small magnitude of error in their estimate.

• In general, different subsystems may perceive the world differently which can cause accidents due to mode confusion. If one subsystem is slower than other subsystems, then this type of mode confusion will exist at certain times. The impacts and effects of mode confusion have been emphasized in [9]. The lack of feedback from a computer system to the operator can cause mode confusion. An example of mode confusion, provided in [9], relates a situation where a human perceives the system to be in one mode and a computer is in another mode; however, this type of mode confusion can also exist between two computers.

• In systems that record sensor datathrough periodic sampling of sensorsbut does not take any action at runtime, if the delay is too large, then a sensor datum may not have been stored before a new sensor datum becomes available and this may cause loss of one sensor datum.
• In a system that gives commands to an actuator, there are often physical limitations on the actuator and this translates into timing requirements on the software (page 10 in [12]).

• For reasons for fault-tolerance, it is common to duplicate hardware and run the same software (replicas) on each of the hardware and then at run-time compare the output produced by the replicas. If the replicas read a sensor at different times, then it can happen that they produce different outputs. In this case, there is not actually a fault but it may be declared as a fault. This can, in turn, trigger the wakeup of a set of other replicas which can suffer from the same issue. Indeed, this caused the incident on China Airlines Flight CI202, Airbus A330-302 in Taiwan on June 14, 2020 [46,47].
In military systems, the importance of timing requirements was recently emphasized in JADC2 by USD A&S Bill LaPlante [30] pointing out that "milliseconds matter."

div.head: C. What causes delays in software executing on single-core?
div.p: Most real-time software is written as a set of threads or processes where each process first performs its initialization and then enters an infinite loop. Each iteration of the infinite loop typically consists of (i) waiting until it is time to execute (e.g., waiting for a timer to expire or waiting for a message to be received), (ii) perform input operation (e.g., read sensor, or read incoming message), (iii) perform processing based on input, and (iv) perform output (e.g., send command to actuator or send message). In C-like code, we can write such a thread as follows: Typically, there are no real-time requirements associated with the initialization but there is typically a real-time requirement on each loop iteration: the time from when the thread/process is requested to execute until it has performed its output must be less than or equal to a pre-specified deadline.

div.head: Fig. 3. Two-step reasoning framework (High-level view).
div.p: Thus, if we can determine an upper bound on the time from when the thread/process is requested to execute until it has performed its actuation command, then we can also determine whether it satisfied its timing requirement (of course we must do this for all threads/processesnot just one thread/process). For convenience, we repeat below the code and show the delay that we are interested in as an arrow: This delay depends on the execution of the thread but it also depends on the time that the thread is prevented from execution because other threads occupy the processor. In addition, there is another term that contributes to the delay; we will discuss this now.

In some cases, a thread needs to perform operations under mutual exclusion with respect to other threads. This is sometimes necessary when performing operations on shared data structures. To understand this, let us modify the aforementioned thread so that after reading the sensor, it reads a shared data structure (e.g., to get a new setpoint from a human operator). To make sure that this reading is performed under mutual exclusion, we lock a semaphore (wait-operation on semaphore) before performing the operation that requires mutual exclusion and unlock when this operation has been completed (signal operation on semaphore). We also indicate the delay that we are interested in as an arrow. This gives us: Note here that we now have additional delays. Clearly the execution of read_shared_data_thread1 takes time; and executing lock and unlock of semaphores take time. But more importantly, when executing lock semaphore, the thread may have to wait. Hence, we can express the delay as having three terms:
• The time for the thread's own execution.
• The time that the thread is interrupted because another thread uses the processor.
• The time that the thread is waiting because the semaphore was locked.

The first term depends on the thread itself. But the two latter terms depend on execution time of other threads and the resource management mechanism. For example, the 2 nd term depends on the CPU scheduler in the operating system; the 3 rd term depends on the queuing discipline used in a lock (e.g., FIFO queuing). In addition, these terms depend on (i) the control flow of the thread, (ii) micro-architectural features that influence the thread itself (a thread may fetch data to its cache so that it executes faster later on), and (iii) micro-architectural features that influence how one thread influences other threads (e.g., one thread evicts a cache block that is used by another thread). Furthermore, a thread may start a DMA transfer which consumes memory bus cycles when another thread executes.

div.head: D. What causes delays in software executing on multi-core?
div.p: The causes of delay that a thread can experience when executing on a multicore includes the cause of delay of a single-core but in addition, a thread can experience the following delay caused by (i) execution of other software on other processor cores (inter-core interference), (ii) execution of other software executing on same processor core (hyperthreading), (iii) activity (e.g., DMA transfer) of other hardware units (Ethernet, I2C, GPUs, hardware accelerators). The following is a list of these causes of delay:

• Cache eviction of L2 cache. There are two possibilities: private L2 cache and shared L2 cache. For the latter, there can clearly be cache eviction. But note that even if the L2 cache is private to a processor core, many chips use hyperthreading and hence may have two or more hardware threads on a single core and these can share the L2 cache even if it is private to the core. • Port contention of L2 cache • Cache eviction of shared L3 cache • Port contention of shared L3 cache • Cache eviction of shared L4 cache (the L4 cache may be implemented in DRAMsee [45]and hence the delay that a program experience may be different than if it was implemented in SRAM. For example, memory access requesting data from an L4 cache implemented with DRAM may suffer from additional delay due to DRAM refresh overhead; also there may be overheads due to the DRAM controller).
• Port contention of shared L4 cache (the L4 cache may be implemented in DRAM; see [45])
• Variations on the above for split caches (e.g., I-cache and D-cache).

• L1 TLB 1 • Refresh overhead in shared L4 cache implemented in DRAM [45] (this is not really an inter-core interference channel but it is an overhead and it impacts timing) • Reordering effect in memory controller (a memory access by one thread can take a long time to be served because another thread accesses memory and the memory controller prioritizes the latter thread)

• Contention on memory bus • Bank conflicts (this is caused by the fact that main memory is organized into memory banks where in each memory bank, there is a row buffer that serves as an internal cache in the memory bank; if a thread accesses adjacent memory accesses in the same memory bank, then this will result in a row-hit and this makes memory accesses faster but of course there can also be row-misses and this becomes more common if two different threads access the same memory bank).
• Additional memory accesses caused by prefetching (this interacts with all the effects mentioned above)
• Additional memory accesses caused by TLB misses (on x86, in the worst-case, this can be severe: 4-5 times as many memory accesses)

• Evictions in miss-status holding register (MSHR). In certain cases, this can cause a severe slowdown of execution (103 times slowdown has been observed [21] and 300 times slowdown has been observed [34]). • Slowdown of execution caused by hyperthreading (simultaneous multithreading) • Slowdown of execution caused by thermal management • Cache misses (in any of the caches mentioned above) caused by cache invalidate messages as part of the cache coherency protocol. It is noteworthy that although L1 caches are typically processor-core private, it is still possible for one cache block in one processor core to be evicted due to execution of a thread on another processor core (because of cache coherency traffic).

• Additional memory accesses (that can cause any of the issues mentioned above) due to DMA traffic. (This is not really an inter-core interference channel but it is an interference channel/overhead and it impacts timing.)

div.head: E. Why analyzing the delay is challenging
div.p: There are many sources of the delay that we are interested in. Furthermore, we are interested in not just finding a delay but we are interested in the worst-case delay (i.e., the maximum delay). That is, we need to deal with corner-cases. It tends to be very hard to achieve this. The current research literature only addresses analysis of delays for a small set of the aforementioned causes. Therefore, it is common to resort to (i) finding an upper bound on the delay rather than finding the maximum delay and (ii) ignore many of these causes. The twostep reasoning framework does exactly that. III. TWO-STEP REASONING FRAMEWORK: OVERVIEW Fig. 3 shows a high-level view of the two-step reasoning framework. Step 1 is find characteristics of each thread/process. Step 2 is make sure that all threads/processes satisfy timing requirements when executing together on a shared computer platform. Step 2 takes as input the output of Step 1.

Fig. 4 shows a more detailed view of the two-step reasoning framework. Here, Step 1 is decomposed into three activities: for each thread/process, find its resource consumption (Section 1.D in [36] points out the importance of this), for each thread/process find its invocation pattern, and for each thread/process determine its timing requirements. This two-step reasoning framework has two advantages.
• The framework is compositional and hence it decreases complexity of the analysis.

• The framework allows us to use different tools and/or techniques in the two steps. Specifically in Step 2, we can use a formal model and mathematical proofs. In Step 1, there are three different areas of activities. Under "find resource characteristic of each thread/process," we can use empirical measurements (e.g., run a thread many times and observe its maximum resource consumption). Under "Find timing requirements of each thread/process," we can read software requirement specifications and extract these timing requirements. Under "Find invocation pattern of each thread/process," we can get this information from inspecting the source code if the thread/process is programmed to arrive periodically.

This two-step reasoning allows a software practitioner to use FM at a self-pace and in an incremental manner. It does not require the use of FMs for all activities. It is also possible to use this two-step reasoning framework without using any FM. In the latter case, Step 2 can be done using a high-level simulator. But later, when a practitioner learns more about FM, then the practitioner can replace Step 2 with a FM. There are many ways in which one can flesh-out the twostep reasoning framework. We discuss some ways in the subsequent sections.

div.head: IV. TWO-STEP REASONING FRAMEWORK: SINGLE-CORE
div.p: A.
Step 1 SEI has developed two tools for Worst-Case Execution-Time (WCET) analysis. This performs the activity "Find resource characteristics of each thread/process."

One tool [15] uses Extreme-Value theory to obtain an estimate of WCET with a confidence level but it is based on running the target program with randomly generated inputs (it does not use any smartness). Another tool [16] attempts to probe the input space to find an input that causes long execution time; this is based on Genetic Algorithms (GA). Thus, it takes advantage of knowledge; if it learns that input i1 causes long execution time and input i2 also causes long execution time, then it can combine i1 and i2 to generate i3 with the intention that i3 should have even longer execution time.

AvMC has developed the MCP GUI (shown in Fig. 6) using LabView, which serves as a valuable tool for analysis on single-and multi-core processors because it enables users to specify which different processor workloads to execute, control the measurement of hardware counter and timing metrics, and transmit the real-time metric measurement data collected back to separately developed analysis tools in Ethernet UDP messages. It also provides the ability to store that data to a log file for archival purposes or pass the data into an Excel spreadsheet for live graphs. Configuration XML files can be employed to handle differences in target boards. The MCP GUI works in conjunction with the MCP Router, which converts DDS Connext© messages to and from Ethernet UDP messages. of communications and their respective messages between the individual MCP analysis tools. Figure 6 is the MCP GUI, the top half showing the cores configuration and the bottom half showing the app configuration.

Note that some of these parameters that describe a thread are context dependent. For example, the WCET of a thread at one processor temperature may be different from the WCET of a thread at another processor temperature. Hence, during a mission, in the early phase, the processor may be cold which may result in a shorter execution time, however later in the mission, the processor may be warm, which may result in a longer execution time for the same process/thread. Also, the temperature the processor experienced during certification testing may be different from the temperature the processor experienced during mission, which is a consideration required for having the system qualified for the various operational conditions of the software as well as the hardware.

div.head: B. Step 2
div.p: SEI has developed a theory that makes it possible to prove mathematically that all timing requirements are satisfied. The main idea is (i) assume that a fixed-priority scheduler is used at run-time and then (ii) for each thread, one can compute an upper bound on the time it needs and the higher-priority threads need and if there is a point before its deadline where the amounts needed is at most the amount of time available, then the deadline is met. This theory is called Rate-Monotonic (RM) scheduling theory [22].

div.head: A. Step 1:
div.p: The SEI tools [15,16] for single core systems can be applied also on multicore. In addition, SEI has developed a tool that use GA to estimate the maximum slowdown that a thread can experience due to co-runner threads on other processor cores [17]. This technique is agnostic to the hardware elements.

AvMC has developed a technique to stress specific hardware units. The MCP GUI as part of its larger framework (shown in Fig. 5) while capable of being applied to single core systems, really showcases its feature set with being applied to multi-core systems. Fig. 6 shows the GUI. The Metric Mapping Section of the GUI allows the user to select the hardware metrics to collect at a specified rate, which is configurable per core. The Event Mapping Section allows the user to select different software applications to run on each core, such as cache misses, with additional options for the timing partition and frequency. The framework can support the batch running of scenarios, pitting applications running concurrently on separate cores against each other, to study the timing and hardware effects from the consequential sharing of resources, or interference. The collection of timing and hardware metrics through this drives the characterization of the interference with respect to the severity of the slowdown and the way in which it arises.

Earlier DASC papers [36,37,38] have studied interferencegeneration for multicore. Note that the two-step process in [38] is different from our two-step reasoning framework. [39] studies aircraft functions that can benefit from multicore but does not discuss certification. Real-time software executing on multicore has been studied in CAST-32A [40]; it provides design guidance and objectives but does not provide FM tools or theories and does not provide any two-step reasoning framework. [41] discusses real-time software on multicore; it takes a traditional safety approach (hazard analysis+mitigation strategy) and does not present any FM or framework that allows incorporation of FMs.

div.head: B. Step 2:
div.p: SEI has developed a RM scheduling theory also for multicore [18,19]. This relies on fixed-priority preemptive scheduling without ARINC 653 time partitioning. But the work in [19] has recently been extended to also support ARINC 653 time partitioning [31].

div.head: VI. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: Current certification guidance documents for aircraft provide plans, processes, and objectives. This has been successful in terms of achieving safety but it comes at the expense of leading to a less agile software development; this makes software development slow for greenfield development, prevents rapid updates of software, and prevents rapid upgrades of hardware. The use of formal methods (FM) has the potential to avoid some of these drawbacks. A critical issue today is the use of multicore and their potential to introduce inter-core interference which can violate real-time requirements. Therefore, in this paper, we have presented a two-step reasoning framework that can be used to bring some FM to analysis of real-time requirements of software executing on multicore.

The two-step reasoning framework presented here can be used as described, however it can also be used to support two Engineering) [23], and (ii) assurance cases [24]. Regarding the latter, it is worth noting that a FM can be used as a strategy (as it is called in Goal Structuring Notation) which takes lowerlevel goals and uses these to support a higher-level goal. FM can also be viewed as a new form of tracing. In normal tracing, a higher-level requirement is traced to lower-level requirements; with FM, we can view a guarantee provided by FM as traced to its assumptions. Some systems support many modes and have many different configurations. (The importance of configurations is emphasized in Section 7.0 Software Configuration Management Process in [1] and a specific example highlighting the importance of configuration is available in [35].) If this is the case, then the two-step reasoning framework can be applied on each combination of mode-configuration.

Regarding the latter, it is worth noting that a FM can be used as a strategy (as it is called in Goal Structuring Notation) which takes lowerlevel goals and uses these to support a higher-level goal. FM can also be viewed as a new form of tracing. In normal tracing, a higher-level requirement is traced to lower-level requirements; with FM, we can view a guarantee provided by FM as traced to its assumptions.
